chunks: ʿAlī ibn Ibrāhīm narrated from his father, from Ibn Faḍḍāl and Muḥammad ibn ʿĪsā, from Yūnus, all together from al-Riḍā عليه السلام; and Sahl ibn Ziyād from al-Ḥasan ibn Ẓarīf, from his father Ẓarīf ibn Nāṣiḥ, from ʿAbd Allāh ibn Ayyūb, from Abī ʿAmr al-Mutaṭabbib, who said:

I presented to Abī ʿAbd Allāh عليه السلام what Amīr al-Muʾminīn عليه السلام had ruled regarding blood-money. Among what he had ruled regarding the body, he made it six assessed categories: the life, sight, hearing, speech, diminution of light from the eye, hoarseness, and paralysis in the hands and feet.

Then he assigned with each of these a qasāmah in accordance with the amount its diyah reached. He set the qasāmah for a life in intentional killing at fifty men, and for a life in accidental killing at twenty-five men. For injuries of the limbs whose diyah reached one thousand dinars, he set six persons, and whatever was less than that was according to its proportion out of six persons.

The qasāmah in life, hearing, sight, intellect, the light of the eye, hoarseness, and impairment of the hands and feet is based on six parts of the man. Its explanation is this: when a man is afflicted in one of these six parts, that is measured. If it is one-sixth of his sight, hearing, speech, or other than that, he swears by himself alone. If it is one-third of his sight, he swears and one man swears with him. If it is half of his sight, he swears and two men swear with him. If it is two-thirds of his sight, he swears and three men swear with him. If it is five-sixths, he swears and four men swear with him. If it is all of his sight, he swears and five men swear with him.

Likewise, all qasāmah in wounds is in this manner. If the injured person has no one to swear with him, the oaths are multiplied upon him: if it is one-sixth of his sight, he swears once; if it is one-third, he swears over it twice; if it is half, he swears three times; if it is two-thirds, he swears four times; if it is five-sixths, he swears five times; and if it is all of it, he swears six times, then he is given [the compensation].

key_terms.الدِّيَاتِ: blood-money compensations for homicide or bodily injury
key_terms.السَّمْعُ: hearing, treated as a compensable faculty
key_terms.النَّفْسُ: the life of the person, as a legal subject of diyah
key_terms.الْأَيْمَانُ: the oaths required in the qasāmah procedure
key_terms.الْبَصَرُ: sight or vision, assessed as a compensable faculty
key_terms.الْجَوَارِحِ: limbs or bodily members for which injury compensation is assessed
key_terms.الْعَقْلِ: intellect, counted among the protected human faculties in legal compensation
key_terms.الْقَسَامَةَ: a formal procedure of sworn oaths used in proving certain injury or killing claims

ai.seo_question: How is qasāmah calculated in Shia fiqh for bodily injuries and partial loss of faculties?
ai.summary: This hadith records legal rulings attributed to Amīr al-Muʾminīn عليه السلام concerning diyah and qasāmah in cases of homicide and bodily injury. It explains how the required number of oaths is proportioned to the degree of injury, especially in relation to sight, hearing, speech, intellect, and limb impairment, and how the injured person may repeat oaths when no supporting swearers are available.
